summary: Scientists put a salt marsh in a giant wave-machine: here's what they learned. An AI tool improves weather forecasts up to a month ahead. Using AI to offer personalized health advice.

facts.statement: Fact 1: Scientists put a salt marsh in a giant wave-machine: here's what they learned.
Fact 2: An AI tool improves weather forecasts up to a month ahead.
Fact 3: Using AI to offer personalized health advice.

sources.title: Scientists put a salt marsh in a giant wave-machine: here's what they learned
sources.description:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03376-6

Experiment shows how these ecosystems could protect coastlines from huge storms — plus, new evidence hints at what Denisovans might have looked like.

sources.title: An AI tool improves weather forecasts up to a month ahead
sources.description:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03077-0

An innovative artificial-intelligence application enhances weather forecasting in the difficult subseasonal range, providing accurate forecasts of precipitation, temperature and pressure 3–5 weeks in advance. The tool refines both physics- and AI-based weather models and improves the early prediction of extremes of heat, cold, rainfall and flooding.

sources.title: Using AI to offer personalized health advice
sources.description:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03065-4

The use of artificial-intelligence tools in medicine is increasing. What types of technology might be on the horizon and how can such health-advice tools be tested?

sources.title: Global emissions slow — but world hurtles towards 2 °C of warming
sources.description:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03355-x

The United Nations’ latest climate report is a stark reminder that limiting warming to the safest levels is now likely out of reach.

sources.title: Huge mapping study reveals how your brain tracks what your body is feeling
sources.description:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03334-2

Signals in the insula region, deep in the brain, can make people feel hot, tingly and nauseous.

sources.title: Plastics embedded with enzymes degrade readily in the sea
sources.description:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03282-x

Embedding enzymes that break down ester bonds into compostable polyesters enables rapid and complete biodegradation even in microbe-scarce environments. This method is effective in marine sites ranging from coastal sea water to the deep sea, and could therefore contribute towards solving the global plastic pollution problem.

sources.title: The Bursar
sources.description:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03110-2

A good way to learn?

sources.title: This is what the mysterious Denisovans looked like
sources.description:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03360-0

Archaeologists identified skulls from China as belonging to this group of ancient human relatives.

sources.title: Can plants defend coasts against storms?
sources.description:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03063-6

Salt-marsh plants can protect inland areas against huge waves — but seemingly only up to a point, and big storms cause progressive damage.

sources.title: Worms live longer in cool conditions thanks to a muscle-derived molecule
sources.description:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03066-3

In nematodes, a metabolite induced by the cold links low temperatures to a body-wide signal that promotes longevity. This signalling system is also seen in human cells.

sources.title: Cave stalagmites document global patterns in monsoon rainfall over the past 450,000 years
sources.description:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03285-8

A 450,000-year stalagmite record of rainfall in the Amazon Basin , combined with existing Asian records, shows that the global monsoon system has oscillated regularly, strengthening in one hemisphere while weakening in the other. However, during intervals of warmth and warming climate, monsoons in both hemispheres failed for millennia.

sources.title: Large-scale single crystals printed layer by layer
sources.description:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03257-y

A 3D-printing method has made single crystals of metals and alloys in complex shapes and up to one metre in length, as needed for advanced technological applications.

sources.title: A single antimatter particle in a cage opens door to 'revolutionary' physics
sources.description:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03342-2

Physicists trap and cool down positron for months to measure its 'magnetic moment' with extraordinary precision.

sources.title: Robert Williamson obituary: geneticist who mapped genes for muscular dystrophy and cystic fibrosis
sources.description:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03375-7

Researcher and policy adviser who championed tests and treatments for genetic diseases.

sources.title: Fabric user interface can be worn on your sleeve — and machine-washed
sources.description:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03064-5

Touch-sensitive, light-emitting yarn can turn everyday clothing into washable, bendable user interfaces with dynamic graphics and versatile computing functions.

sources.title: How tech billionaires are disrupting biomedical science
sources.description:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03311-9

Money from the world’s increasingly prosperous technology entrepreneurs has been flooding into biomedical research. Is it changing how science is done?

sources.title: How a new wave of science philanthropists can have the greatest impact
sources.description:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03326-2

Tech entrepreneurs are bringing an engineer’s eye to research funding. They must be open about their findings to reap maximum benefit.

sources.title: The contribution of salt marshes to wave attenuation during extreme storms
sources.description:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11145-8

Salt marsh platforms resist erosion under extreme waves, but vegetation damage reduces wave attenuation; substantial wave attenuation by vegetation is mainly limited to low-energy marsh coasts with waves below 1 m.

sources.title: Cold activates a BH2 metabolic network promoting longevity and proteostasis
sources.description:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11152-9

A multi-tissue signalling system links cold temperature to enhanced longevity and proteostasis in Caenorhabditis elegans.

sources.title: Structural basis for protocadherin-1 recognition by New World hantaviruses
sources.description:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11184-1

The structure of PCDH1 bound to the ANDV spike defines the structural determinants of hantavirus–receptor recognition.

sources.title: Additive manufacturing of ultralong and architected single crystals
sources.description:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11185-0

A free-form additive manufacturing method that uses alternating and pulsed heat inputs is described for fabricating metre-tall, centimetre-diameter single crystals of Ti-6Al-4V, as well as hard-to-process refractory metals, including W, Mo, Nb and MoNb alloys.

sources.title: Enzyme-embedded polyesters for accelerated biodegradation in the deep sea
sources.description:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11192-1

Near-complete deep-sea degradation of enzyme-embedded compostable polyesters shows that thermal enzyme embedding greatly accelerates breakdown across marine environments while preserving material performance, offering a promising strategy to mitigate persistent ocean plastic pollution.

sources.title: The anatomy of a personal health agent
sources.description:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11161-8

A multi-agent framework that coordinates data science, medical reasoning and health coaching over longitudinal wearable and clinical data to provide holistic personal health support is described.
